status: Native construction draft; packaging and interactive runner pending

steps.title: Trace a rectangular product before writing loops
steps.prose: Use the two-by-three left input and the three-by-two right input from the worked example. Keep the output row and column fixed while listing the three reduction pairs. This gives a value to check before any register allocation or traversal change. Record the flattened output in row-major order, with an eight-byte slot for each result.
steps.expectedObservation: The four exact output values are 58, 64, 139 and 154.

quiz.prompt: Which values determine output row one, column zero?

choices.text: The second left row and first right column.
The second row of both inputs.
Only the diagonal of each input.

hints.text: Fix one output row and column before following k.
For C[1,0], pair 4,5,6 with 7,9,11.

steps.title: Separate row stride from tile edge
steps.prose: Derive each address from the matrix representation. The left row contains K words; the right and output rows contain N elements of different widths. Tile edge T bounds the work scheduled together and does not repack either input. Use the address table to predict the first three pairs for the second output row.
steps.expectedObservation: The right column advances by 4N bytes and the output row by 8N bytes.

quiz.prompt: What determines the right-input reduction stride?

hints.text: Keep the original packed row widths beside each address formula.
A tile edge limits iteration; it does not become the stride of B.

steps.title: Prove the width of a partial sum
steps.prose: Use two minimum input values in each reduction pair. One product fits a signed word, but adding two such products crosses the signed-word endpoint. The domain allows up to sixteen products per output. Keep the full result from every addition through the final store.
steps.expectedObservation: Two products sum to 2147483648; sixteen sum to 17179869184.

quiz.prompt: Which part must retain more than thirty-two bits?

hints.text: Calculate two minimum-times-minimum products explicitly.
The sum crosses the signed-word endpoint before the individual product does.

steps.title: Inspect the supplied frame and safe exits
steps.prose: The starter supplies both function frames and exits. Each frame saves all nine required full registers, retains the three input pointers, and loads M, K, N and T into working registers. An unfinished region branches to its own restoring exit. These exits calculate the cell count, restore caller registers and return through `ra`. Select the scalar path first; a provisional return is evidence about construction, not a completed matrix product.
steps.expectedObservation: The untouched starter returns four for the default shape while leaving the output sentinel unchanged.

quiz.prompt: When should the saved registers be restored?

choices.text: After releasing the stack frame and overwriting its contents.
Before releasing their private stack storage.

hints.text: Locate the saved slots and the restoring exit before replacing a region.
The provisional branch uses that exit so unfinished code still obeys register preservation.

steps.title: Guard empty scalar output and start row zero
steps.prose: Test the two output dimensions before any matrix operation. A zero row or column count means there are no destination cells. K may still be nonzero, but that does not authorize an input load. For a nonempty output, initialize the row index `t0` to zero. Keep the descriptor loads and frame supplied by the starter.
steps.expectedObservation: Default construction returns with `t0`=0 and unchanged output. Empty M or N performs no matrix access.

quiz.prompt: Which shape needs no output store?

hints.text: Ask whether any output row and column both exist.
Test M and N before entering a body that can load or store a matrix element.

steps.code:
beq $s0, $zero, naive_return
    nop
    beq $s2, $zero, naive_return
    nop
    move $t0, $zero

steps.title: Reset the scalar column at each row
steps.prose: The label `naive_row` is the entry for a new output row. Set `t1` to zero here so every row begins at its first column. This initialization belongs outside the column loop. Placing it inside the column body would repeatedly return the column index to zero.
steps.expectedObservation: The first provisional return has row `t0`=0 and column `t1`=0.

quiz.prompt: Where must column zero be established?

choices.text: At the start of every output row.

hints.text: Separate entering a new row from entering a new cell.
The row label must reset j; the column loop must leave that reset behind.

steps.title: Start a fresh reduction for each output cell
steps.prose: At `naive_column`, clear `t2` for the reduction index and `t3` for its exact accumulator. Every output has a separate sum, even when neighboring outputs share many input values. These initializations will run again when the column loop advances.
steps.expectedObservation: The current sum and reduction index are both zero.

quiz.prompt: Why clear the sum inside the column loop?

choices.text: Every output cell has its own dot product.
The previous sum is always an input operand.

hints.text: Write the invariant for zero products consumed.
Both the reduction index and the accumulator start at zero for every output.

steps.title: Form the full left-row address
steps.prose: Multiply the row index by K to count left-input elements before this row, then multiply that offset by four. Add the byte offset to the full base with `daddu`. The bounded index arithmetic does not permit narrowing the base pointer. Retain this walker in `t4`.
steps.expectedObservation: For the first output, `t4` addresses the first left element.

quiz.prompt: Which factor converts a left-input element offset into bytes?

hints.text: Count elements before row i before converting to bytes.
Use i*K words, scale by four, then add the full left base.

steps.title: Form the right-column address and row stride
steps.prose: The first pair in column j is B[0,j], so multiply `t1` by four and add it to the right base. Keep the resulting walker in `t5`. Compute 4N in `t6` once for this dot product; that stride moves from one right-input row to the next without changing the selected column.
steps.expectedObservation: The first right walker addresses right[0], and `t6` is eight bytes for N=2.

quiz.prompt: What stays fixed as the right walker advances?

hints.text: Follow one fixed column across the physical rows of B.
The first position is column j; successive positions differ by N stored words.

steps.title: Skip the scalar reduction when K is zero
steps.prose: Test K before entering `naive_dot`. A zero reduction has a valid zero sum and still needs output stores for every selected cell. Branch to `naive_store`, retaining the cleared accumulator. The input walkers may have been computed, but computing an address is not a memory access.
steps.expectedObservation: With K=0, the provisional sum is zero and neither matrix is read.

quiz.prompt: What is the output of a nonempty zero-reduction product?

hints.text: An empty sum has a value even when no input pair exists.
Bypass the pair loads for K=0 and continue toward the output store with a zero accumulator.

steps.title: Load one signed left value
steps.prose: At `naive_dot`, use `lw` to load the signed word through `t4`. The input domain is signed sixteen-bit, but each stored element occupies a complete word. The load sign-extends that stored signed value into the full register. Keep the right operand separate in the next edit.
steps.expectedObservation: The default first left operand is 1. A minimum operand remains -32768 in the full register.

quiz.prompt: How should stored -32768 be interpreted?

hints.text: The value is stored in a word even though its numerical range is narrower.
Use a signed word load; the register must retain a negative input as a negative full-width value.

steps.title: Load the matching signed right value
steps.prose: Load the right word through `t5` into `t8`. Both walkers refer to the same reduction position: one row value in A and one column value in B. Do not advance either walker between these two loads. The multiplication that follows consumes this pair.
steps.expectedObservation: For the first default pair, `t7`=1 and `t8`=7.

quiz.prompt: Which pair belongs to reduction position zero?

choices.text: A[0,0] and B[0,0] for the first output.

hints.text: Match the same reduction position in both inputs.
Keep the left operand in `t7` while loading the right operand through its separate walker.

steps.title: Compute the exact signed product
steps.prose: Multiply the two full signed operands with `dmul` and retain the result in `t7`. It is safe to overwrite the loaded left operand after its product is formed; the next iteration reloads the next value. This edit does not yet add the product to the sum.
steps.expectedObservation: The first product is 7. Two minimum operands produce 1073741824.

quiz.prompt: Can the loaded left operand be replaced by its product here?

choices.text: No; it is the immutable source memory.
Yes; the register value has already been consumed.
Only if the product is zero.

hints.text: Distinguish the loaded operand from the memory it came from.
After forming the product, the left-operand register can hold that product; the input memory remains unchanged.

steps.title: Add the product to the full scalar sum
steps.prose: Use `daddu` to add `t7` into `t3`. The width proof ensures that every allowed partial sum fits; no product bits are discarded by this 64-bit addition. Advance the loop only after the current product has contributed.
steps.expectedObservation: After one default pair, `t3`=7 and the reduction index is still zero.

quiz.prompt: What does the sum contain immediately after this edit?

hints.text: Track how many products the sum represents before incrementing k.
Add the full product into `t3` with a doubleword addition.

steps.title: Consume the row and column until K products are complete
steps.prose: Advance the left walker by four and the right walker by 4N, then increment `t2`. Continue at `naive_dot` while the index differs from K. The pre-entry zero test and unit increments make equality sufficient for this bounded loop. At exit, `t3` includes exactly K products.
steps.expectedObservation: The first default sum is 58 after three products; a two-term minimum-value case sums to 2147483648.

quiz.prompt: When is the scalar sum complete?

hints.text: Each iteration consumes one row value and one column value.
Advance A by one word, B by one full right row, and repeat until k reaches K.

steps.code:
daddiu $t4, $t4, 4
    daddu $t5, $t5, $t6
    addiu $t2, $t2, 1
    bne $t2, $s1, naive_dot
    nop

steps.title: Address the current doubleword output
steps.prose: At `naive_store`, compute row*N+column, multiply by eight, then add the output base. Reuse `t4` only now that the reduction no longer needs its left walker. The output index uses N, whereas the left-input row index used K.
steps.expectedObservation: The first output address is the supplied product base.

quiz.prompt: Why shift the output offset by three?

choices.text: The input words have eight bytes.

hints.text: Output cells are twice as wide as input words.
Use i*N+j as the element index and scale it by eight before adding C.

steps.title: Store both halves of the completed output
steps.prose: Store `t3` with `sd` through the current output address. The full cell is now public output. Other output cells retain the sentinel until their dot products are processed. Inspect both words for a result whose exact value exceeds signed-word range.
steps.expectedObservation: Only the first default cell is now 58; the other three remain sentinel.

quiz.prompt: What must an output store preserve?

choices.text: All eight bytes of the exact result.

hints.text: Inspect the high word of the two-product boundary result.
A full result needs a doubleword store even when the default small example fits a word.

steps.title: Advance the scalar column and restart its reduction
steps.prose: Increment `t1` and branch to `naive_column` while another column remains. That target resets both the reduction index and the accumulator, then reconstructs both input walkers for the new column. A completed row ends with `t1`=N.
steps.expectedObservation: The first default output row is now 58,64; the second row is still sentinel.

quiz.prompt: Which state must restart for the next output column?

choices.text: The reduction index, accumulator and input walkers.

hints.text: A new column starts a new dot product.
Branch to the column initialization so its sum and both walkers restart.

steps.title: Advance the scalar row and complete the baseline
steps.prose: Increment `t0` and continue at `naive_row` while another output row remains. The row label resets the column index; the column label resets the dot product. On completion, fall through to the supplied restoring exit. Test this complete scalar stage against behavior, including empty dimensions and full-width results.
steps.expectedObservation: All four default outputs are 58,64,139,154 and `v0` reports four.

quiz.prompt: Why target `naive_row` after changing the row?

choices.text: It resets the column for the new row.
It restores every output to sentinel.
It repeats the previous row address.

hints.text: The old row has already consumed all columns.
Return to the row label so the next row begins again at column zero.

steps.title: Select the tiled function without changing the contract
steps.prose: Use the tiled input recipes to select method one in a separate observation file. Keep the cumulative source method word at its default zero so prepare.py can apply either method reproducibly. Function grading can invoke either entry directly; the selector is a convenience for the program caller. Keep the baseline as a checked comparison. Both functions take the same pointer descriptor and return the same cell count.
steps.expectedObservation: Switching the selector changes which function runs; it does not change the matrix representation.

quiz.prompt: What changes when the selector becomes one?

choices.text: The word width of both inputs.
The right matrix is automatically transposed.

hints.text: Keep the source used for preparing recipes at its documented defaults.
The recipe writes method one into a separate observation file for the tiled entry.

steps.title: Guard empty tiled output
steps.prose: Perform the same M and N checks before zeroing the product. Tile boundaries and reduction reads are irrelevant when no output cell exists. Keep this guard ahead of the zeroing loop, whose body must not execute for a zero output count.
steps.expectedObservation: Empty M or N leaves every output byte unchanged and performs no matrix access.

quiz.prompt: May an empty output call clear the first product cell?

choices.text: No; there is no selected output cell.
Yes; mapped memory is always writable.

hints.text: Consider an output interval of length zero.
Place both output-dimension tests before the first zeroing store.

steps.code:
beq $s0, $zero, tiled_return
    nop
    beq $s2, $zero, tiled_return
    nop

steps.title: Count the product cells to initialize
steps.prose: Compute M*N in `t0` and copy the full output base to `t1`. This count is a number of doublewords, not bytes. The output pointer will advance by eight for each zeroed cell. Prior output contents may come from another call and cannot serve as initial sums.
steps.expectedObservation: The default zeroing count is four and `t1` addresses the supplied product.

quiz.prompt: What unit does the zeroing counter use?

hints.text: Keep the units of the counter and pointer separate.
Count M*N cells while the pointer moves eight bytes for each cell.

steps.title: Initialize one full output cell
steps.prose: At `zero_product`, write a doubleword zero. This establishes the first partial sum without reading the previous output. The next edit will repeat it for every selected cell. All eight bytes matter because a later `ld` consumes the full partial sum.
steps.expectedObservation: Only the first default output cell is zero; the rest remain sentinel.

quiz.prompt: Why initialize before reading a partial sum?

choices.text: A previous call always produced the same answer.
The caller grants arbitrary initial output contents.

hints.text: A partial-sum load will later read all eight bytes.
Initialize the entire doubleword without reading its old contents.

steps.title: Initialize the complete product interval
steps.prose: Advance the zeroing pointer by eight, decrement the remaining cell count and repeat while nonzero. The preceding empty-output guard ensures the first iteration exists. At completion, every selected product byte is initialized, with no prefix or suffix writes.
steps.expectedObservation: All four default cells are zero, `t0`=0, and `t1` is 32 bytes beyond the selected output start.

quiz.prompt: Which bytes may this loop clear?

hints.text: The zeroing body handles one complete cell per visit.
Advance by eight and subtract one cell; the empty-output guard handles the zero-iteration case.

steps.title: Return a zero reduction or start the first row tile
steps.prose: After zeroing, return immediately when K is zero. For a nonzero reduction, initialize the row-tile start `s7` to zero. This start is private working state and will be restored to the caller value by the supplied exit; do not confuse the returned saved register with the internal tile start.
steps.expectedObservation: K=0 produces a complete zero matrix without either input read.

quiz.prompt: When does a zero-reduction product become complete?

choices.text: After every selected output cell is zeroed.
After loading one input from each matrix.

hints.text: The zeroing work already gives the answer for an empty reduction.
Return after zeroing when K=0; otherwise establish the first row-tile start.

steps.title: Clip the row-tile exclusive end
steps.prose: At `block_row`, form I+T in `a0`. Compare it with M and retain the smaller value. Keep the start in `s7` separate from the exclusive end. This test must work for a short matrix as well as for the final row tile of a larger matrix.
steps.expectedObservation: For M=2,T=2, `a0`=2. For M=1,T=3, the clipped end is one.

quiz.prompt: Which row index is excluded from this tile?

hints.text: Write the half-open row interval before coding the comparison.
Choose the smaller of I+T and M without changing the stored start I.

steps.code:
addu $a0, $s7, $s3
    sltu $t9, $s0, $a0
    beq $t9, $zero, row_bound
    nop
    move $a0, $s0

steps.title: Reset the column-tile start for each row band
steps.prose: At `row_bound`, set `fp` to zero as the column-tile start J. The frame has already saved the incoming `fp` value, so this temporary role does not change the public preservation requirement. The reset runs once for each new row band.
steps.expectedObservation: The first column tile begins at zero; caller `fp` is restored on provisional return.

quiz.prompt: Why is using `fp` here compatible with the interface?

choices.text: Its incoming full value is saved and restored.
It is always zero on entry.

hints.text: Every new row band needs all of the output columns.
Reset J to zero after calculating the row end, before entering its first column tile.

steps.title: Clip the column-tile exclusive end
steps.prose: At `block_column`, form J+T in `a1` and clip it against N. The output and right input share this column bound. Their element widths differ, but neither width changes the index comparison. Keep the full output pointer in `s6`.
steps.expectedObservation: For N=2,T=2, `a1`=2. A single-column matrix clips to one even when T=3.

quiz.prompt: Which dimension clips the column end?

hints.text: The right and output matrices share a column count.
Clip J+T against N, keeping element width out of the index comparison.

steps.code:
addu $a1, $fp, $s3
    sltu $t9, $s2, $a1
    beq $t9, $zero, column_bound
    nop
    move $a1, $s2

steps.title: Restart the reduction tiles for this output tile
steps.prose: At `column_bound`, set `t0` to zero for L, the first reduction-tile start. Each output tile needs the complete reduction dimension. Carrying L from the previous output tile would skip contributions or bypass its reduction entirely.
steps.expectedObservation: The current output tile begins its reduction at L=0.

quiz.prompt: When should the reduction-tile start return to zero?

choices.text: At the start of each output tile.

hints.text: A different output tile has not yet received any dot-product segments.
Restart L at zero for every new output tile.

steps.title: Clip the reduction-tile exclusive end
steps.prose: At `block_reduction`, form L+T in `a2` and clip it against K. This endpoint controls the number of products contributed in the current tile. A complete last tile is allowed; a shorter last tile must stop before reading an absent input pair.
steps.expectedObservation: The first default reduction tile ends at two. For K=1,T=3, `a2` clips to one.

quiz.prompt: What bounds the last reduction pair?

choices.text: The size of the mapped data segment.

hints.text: Consider K smaller than T and K not divisible by T.
Clip L+T against K so the segment stops at the final real pair.

steps.code:
addu $a2, $t0, $s3
    sltu $t9, $s1, $a2
    beq $t9, $zero, reduction_bound
    nop
    move $a2, $s1

steps.title: Start the current output row at I
steps.prose: At `reduction_bound`, copy `s7` into `t1` for the current row i. Every reduction tile revisits the selected output tile from its first row. The tile start I is independent of the reduction start L held in `t0`.
steps.expectedObservation: The first tile begins with current row `t1`=0.

quiz.prompt: Which start initializes the current output row?

hints.text: The outer tile start and inner current row are distinct state.
Copy I into i at the beginning of each reduction tile.

steps.title: Start the current output column at J
steps.prose: At `blocked_row`, copy `fp` into `t2` for column j. This reset happens for each row in the output tile. The later column loop advances `t2` until the clipped column end `a1`.
steps.expectedObservation: The first tile begins with current column `t2`=0.

quiz.prompt: Why reset j for every row?

choices.text: The previous row consumed its selected columns.
The right matrix has become transposed.

hints.text: Each row in a tile needs its whole selected column interval.
Copy J into j whenever the row loop starts a new row.

steps.title: Address the current output partial sum
steps.prose: At `blocked_column`, compute i*N+j, multiply by eight, and add the full C base. Keep this address in `t7` while the reduction uses `t5` and `t6` as input walkers. The same output cell will be revisited for later L values.
steps.expectedObservation: For the first tile and cell, `t7` addresses the selected product start.

quiz.prompt: Which index expression identifies this cell?

hints.text: Keep this output address available through the complete segment.
Form i*N+j and scale by eight; retain the result in the dedicated C walker.

steps.title: Reload the initialized partial sum
steps.prose: Load the complete doubleword through `t7` into `t4`. For L=0 it is the zero established by the initialization loop. For later reduction tiles it is the sum already contributed by earlier positions. Clearing `t4` here would silently erase that earlier work.
steps.expectedObservation: The first partial sum is zero; later tiles must reload their existing contribution.

quiz.prompt: What belongs in the accumulator before a later reduction tile?

choices.text: The already accumulated output partial sum.

hints.text: Think about what the second reduction tile must preserve.
Load the previously stored full sum, which is zero only on the first segment.

steps.title: Address the left input at the reduction-tile start
steps.prose: Compute i*K+L, scale by four, and add the A base. This walker begins at the current reduction tile rather than at zero. It must be reconstructed for every output cell because the previous dot segment advanced its own walker.
steps.expectedObservation: For the first default reduction tile, `t5` addresses the first left word.

quiz.prompt: Which reduction index belongs in this start address?

hints.text: The segment begins at L rather than reduction position zero.
Address A[i,L] using the physical left row width K.

steps.title: Address the right input at the same reduction start
steps.prose: Compute L*N+j, scale by four, and add the B base. The two walkers now agree on reduction position L. Use the full physical row width N even when the tile contains fewer columns.
steps.expectedObservation: For the first default cell, `t6` addresses the first right word.

quiz.prompt: Why use N in L*N+j?

choices.text: A tile has repacked the right input.
N is the actual right-input row width.

hints.text: Use the same L in the two input starts.
Address B[L,j] with row width N; T has not changed the representation.

steps.title: Retain the right stride and current reduction index
steps.prose: Compute 4N in `a3` and copy L to `t3`. The descriptor pointer originally arrived in `a3`, but all four fields have already been loaded into saved working registers. Reusing `a3` here is safe under the interface and avoids another private slot.
steps.expectedObservation: For the default first segment, `a3`=8 and `t3`=0.

quiz.prompt: Why can `a3` hold a stride now?

choices.text: The descriptor fields are already retained elsewhere.
Arguments are never needed by a function.

hints.text: The original descriptor pointer is no longer needed after its fields are retained.
Reuse its argument register for 4N and initialize k from L.

steps.title: Load the matched pair inside this tile
steps.prose: At `blocked_dot`, load signed words through `t5` and `t6` into `t8` and `t9`. These two values have the same current reduction index. Keep the existing partial sum `t4` unchanged until their exact product is ready.
steps.expectedObservation: The first default tile loads operands 1 and 7, retaining `t4`=0.

quiz.prompt: What does `t4` represent before these operands are added?

hints.text: Leave the existing accumulator untouched while fetching operands.
Load a signed word from each walker at the same reduction position.

steps.title: Form a full product for the tiled sum
steps.prose: Multiply `t8` by `t9` with `dmul`, retaining the product in `t8`. The exact arithmetic is the same as in the scalar baseline; blocking changes when pairs are visited, not how they are multiplied.
steps.expectedObservation: The first default tiled product is 7.

quiz.prompt: Does changing tile edge alter the product arithmetic?

choices.text: Yes; a larger tile requires rounding.
No; the same signed values are multiplied.

hints.text: Blocking changes traversal, while the arithmetic domain remains fixed.
Multiply the signed operands into a full product before adding it to the retained sum.

steps.title: Extend the retained output sum
steps.prose: Add the product to `t4` with `daddu`. For a later reduction tile this addition extends the sum reloaded from C. The completed value will be stored only after the clipped segment ends.
steps.expectedObservation: After the first default pair, the private sum `t4`=7 while output remains zero.

quiz.prompt: When does this new private sum become visible in C?

choices.text: When the tile bound is calculated.

hints.text: At a later segment, the accumulator already includes previous contributions.
Extend `t4` with the current product; do not replace `t4` with the product.

steps.title: Consume exactly the clipped reduction segment
steps.prose: Advance the walkers, increment `t3` and continue at `blocked_dot` until `a2`. The bound is an exclusive original reduction index, not a number of products remaining. The initial `t3`=L ensures this loop consumes only the current segment.
steps.expectedObservation: The first default segment consumes k=0 and k=1, leaving `t4`=25 and `t3`=2.

quiz.prompt: What does `a2` hold in this loop?

hints.text: The endpoint is an original reduction index, not a segment length.
Start k at L and stop at the clipped end after advancing both physical walkers.

steps.code:
daddiu $t5, $t5, 4
    daddu $t6, $t6, $a3
    addiu $t3, $t3, 1
    bne $t3, $a2, blocked_dot
    nop

steps.title: Publish this segment contribution
steps.prose: Store `t4` through the output address retained in `t7`. This value may still be a partial result because more reduction tiles can remain. The public function is complete only after all contributions and all selected output cells have been processed.
steps.expectedObservation: The first default output cell becomes 25; the other three are still zero.

quiz.prompt: Is this segment store always the final output value?

choices.text: Only if it is the last reduction segment for that cell.
Yes; a tile contains the entire matrix.
No; no partial sum may ever be stored.

hints.text: The public output can temporarily hold an incomplete dot product.
Store the full segment sum through the C pointer retained before the input walks.

steps.title: Visit every selected column in the current row
steps.prose: Increment `t2` and continue at `blocked_column` until the clipped column end `a1`. Reconstruct each cell address and input walkers, and reload that cell own partial sum. The first default row has two selected columns.
steps.expectedObservation: The first segment now produces 25,28 in row zero; row one remains zero.

quiz.prompt: Which state must remain independent between neighboring cells?

hints.text: Neighboring cells have independent partial sums.
Restart the cell body for each j until the clipped column endpoint.

steps.title: Visit every selected row in this output tile
steps.prose: Increment `t1` and continue at `blocked_row` until `a0`. That label resets j to J for each row. At this stage the current output tile has received exactly one reduction segment, while other output tiles remain initialized to zero.
steps.expectedObservation: For the default first segment, C is 25,28,73,82.

quiz.prompt: What does the next reduction tile need from this state?

choices.text: The stored partial sum of each output cell.

hints.text: The next row must begin at J again.
Advance i and branch to the row label, which resets the current column.

steps.title: Advance L and retain earlier tile contributions
steps.prose: Add T to the reduction start `t0` and repeat `block_reduction` while L<K. Recompute the clipped reduction end and revisit the current output tile. Each cell reloads its earlier partial sum before consuming the new segment. The default final segment has one product.
steps.expectedObservation: The default product becomes 58,64,139,154 after both reduction tiles.

quiz.prompt: What would resetting the partial sum at this stage discard?

hints.text: The next group contributes to the same output cells.
Advance L by T, reclip its end, and reload every stored partial sum.

steps.title: Advance J and restart its full reduction

steps.title: Advance I and finish all output tiles

steps.prose: Keep arithmetic grading separate from a requested strategy demonstration. An independent i-k-j solution can satisfy the final contract while using a different address schedule.
